items.ig_caption:
The AI ran the intrusion. A human just approved each step. 🤖

SOCRadar found exposed infrastructure from affiliates of the INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups:
→ An AI framework called Phantom executed the intrusions; the operator reviewed every step ("AI-executed, human-approved")
→ About 62 organizations targeted, over half in the US
→ Way in: exploited edge and remote-access systems such as FortiClient EMS, SimpleHelp, cPanel and VPN gateways
→ When a model refused, the operator reframed the request as an "authorized red team assessment"
→ In one case, one reused password unlocked the VPN, servers, RMM, backup and security tools

What to do: patch internet-facing remote-access tools first, give every admin tool its own password plus MFA, and alert on new drivers and reverse-SOCKS tunnels.

cover.hook: 70,000+ credentials exposed. The way in: firewalls and VPNs.
cover.sub: Group-IB and NyxLab tracked "k0t" breaking into FortiGate and GlobalProtect edge devices around the world.

slides.title: Who is k0t?
slides.body: An actor also known as CryptoFeel, Member19 and QazWsxShop, first seen in October 2025. Researchers assess links to the Qilin and The Gentlemen ransomware groups, possibly as an access broker or affiliate.

slides.title: How they got in
slides.body: Scanning for exposed VPN and firewall appliances, then exploiting CVE-2025-64446 (FortiWeb path traversal) and CVE-2026-0257 (PAN-OS and Prisma Access auth bypass), plus brute-forcing common passwords.

slides.label: credentials exposed from network devices and LDAP dumps
slides.note: Nearly 38% of victims in Asia Pacific, 31.9% in Latin America

slides.title: Then they stayed
slides.body: Remote access tools such as MeshCentral, Atera and AnyDesk for persistence, Mimikatz and Impacket to move and steal credentials, and Rclone to copy data out to Wasabi and MEGA.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Patch the FortiWeb and PAN-OS flaws named in the report
Reset credentials stored on or synced to edge devices
Alert on new RMM tools you didn't install
Watch for Rclone traffic to cloud storage

Node2Shell, CVE-2026-111497 (CVSS 4.0: 9.2): a Brotli decoder bug hitting Node.js, Bun, Python Brotli, Envoy and Istio. No exploitation seen yet. Fix: Node 22.23.4 / 24.22.1 / 26.12.1, Bun 1.4.4, then restart and rebuild.

#PatchNow #InfoSec
items.ig_caption:
One compression bug. Node.js, Bun, Python, Envoy and Istio. ⚙️

CVE-2026-111497, nicknamed Node2Shell, sits in Google's Brotli decoder:
→ Crafted compressed data can write past the end of a buffer: crash, memory leak or code execution
→ Rated 9.2 by Google (CVSS 4.0), 8.1 by Red Hat
→ Imperva showed code execution on one Node.js 24.22.0 build; CISA lists exploitation as "none" so far
→ Found by OpenAI's Codex Security team

Do this now: update to Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1, Bun 1.4.4, Python Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0. Then restart services and rebuild container images: running processes keep the old decoder.

cover.hook: One CA private key was the number 4.
cover.sub: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA keys could be computed from public certificates. Browsers, Go and Node.js shipped emergency blocks.

slides.title: What went wrong
slides.body: eMudhra says a step in an April 2025 key ceremony produced weak keys. Researcher Scott Helme reported one private key was the number 4 instead of a random 384-bit number. The flaw went unnoticed for 18 months and passed two audits.

slides.label: for Scott Helme to recover all 8 private keys
slides.note: From the public certificates alone, per The Hacker News

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: With those keys, anyone could issue HTTPS certificates for sites they don't own. Chrome found no TLS certificates from the six TLS intermediates in CT logs before its block. Whether anyone misused them is not known.

slides.title: The response
slides.body: Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, Microsoft and Android blocked the certificates. Go, Node.js, certifi, Ubuntu and Debian shipped fixes. eMudhra says it is leaving the global SSL/TLS business. Chrome drops its emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from 27 Oct.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Update Go to 1.27.3 or 1.26.10 and rebuild
Update ca-certificates and trust bundles everywhere
Find any certs chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3
Move them to another CA before 27 Oct

eMudhra: 8 intermediate CA private keys were weak enough to compute from the public certs. One key was the number 4. Browsers, Go, Node.js and Linux distros shipped emergency blocks.

The week's lessons 🧵 #PKI #CyberSecurity
x_thread:
eMudhra: 8 intermediate CA private keys were weak enough to compute from the public certs. One key was the number 4. Browsers, Go, Node.js and Linux distros shipped emergency blocks.

The week's lessons 🧵 #PKI #CyberSecurity

1/ eMudhra says one step in an April 2025 key ceremony produced weak keys. It went unnoticed for 18 months and passed two audits, until a researcher reverse engineered them. Scott Helme says he recovered all 8 keys in under a second.

2/ Why it matters: with a CA key, an attacker can issue HTTPS certs for sites they don't control. Chrome found no TLS certs from the six TLS intermediates in CT logs before its block. Whether anyone misused them is not known.

3/ Response was fast: Chrome and Mozilla blocked the TLS intermediates on 17 Oct; Apple, Android and Microsoft followed. Go 1.27.3 / 1.26.10 and Node.js 22.23.4 / 24.22.1 / 26.12.1 reject the keys. eMudhra is exiting the global SSL/TLS business.

4/ Same week, same lesson: one shared library, many copies. Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) in the Brotli decoder hits Node.js, Bun, Python, Envoy and Istio. Each must patch its own copy, and running processes keep the old code.

5/ Do this week: update Go and rebuild; update ca-certificates and trust bundles; find certs chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 and move them before Chrome drops it on 27 Oct; update Node.js and restart.

6/ Question: does your app trust its own bundled root store, and who updates it?

Sources: The Hacker News (22 and 24 Oct), The Record (22 Oct).

OpenCode Console breach: an intruder reached a legacy system and OpenAI, Anthropic and Google API keys saved by 1.4% of Console users may be exposed. Users report surprise bills. Revoke at the provider; deleting isn't enough.

#AISecurity #DataBreach
items.ig_caption:
A breach, then surprise AI bills. 💸

OpenCode says an intruder reached a legacy system on the night of 16 Oct:
→ OpenAI, Anthropic and Google API keys saved in its hosted Console may have been exposed
→ 1.4% of Console users affected; keys kept in the CLI and desktop apps are not part of it
→ Users report unexpected usage, one of them $1,700 (user claims, not confirmed by OpenCode)
→ OpenCode says it is working with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google

What to do: an API key is a bearer credential. Deleting it from a tool does not revoke it. Revoke it in the provider dashboard, issue a new one, check billing back to 16 Oct, and set spend limits with one key per tool.
